Saving Private Rhino

By: Julian Sun | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
We reveal the fate of the largest privately owned white rhino herd in the world

Unique Selling Point:
Africa’s beleaguered rhinos have been thrown a significant lifeline with the announcement that nearly 2,000 semi-wild rhinos owned by South African rhino breeder John Hume will be “rewilded” into reserves across South Africa and other parts of the continent over the next 10 years.

African Parks, a private Johannesburg-based conservation NGO that manages 22 protected areas in partnership with 12 governments across Africa, confirmed on Monday, 4 September that it had “stepped in as the new owner of the world’s largest private captive rhino breeding operation”, the Platinum Rhino project, a 7,800-hectare property in North West.

Summary:
African Parks has one clear objective: to rewild these rhino over the next 10 years to well-managed and secure areas, establishing or supplementing strategic populations, thereby de-risking the future of the species. The breeding programme will be phased out and the project will end once all the rhino are released into the wild. This is one of the largest continent-wide rewilding endeavours to occur for any species.

Further information:
As a result of financial stress, Platinum Rhino was put up for auction on the 26th of April 2023, but did not receive any bids, putting these rhinos at serious risk of poaching and fragmentation. Given African Parks’ experience in effectively managing protected areas and carrying out wildlife translocations at scale, including bringing rhino back to Rwanda, Malawi and the Democratic Republic of Congo, African Parks was approached by numerous concerned individuals from the conservation sector to provide a solution to prevent a potential conservation crisis, and to help secure the future for a species in decline.

After conducting a thorough due diligence and with the support of the South African Government, as well as having secured emergency funding to make the transaction possible, African Parks agreed to purchase the farm and all 2,000 rhino. African Parks has one clear objective: to rewild these rhino over the next 10 years to well-managed and secure areas, establishing or supplementing strategic populations, thereby de-risking the future of the species. The breeding programme will be phased out and the project will end once all the rhino are released into the wild. This is one of the largest continent-wide rewilding endeavours to occur for any species.

TX Date:


0000-00-00

Press Release:


Poaching has decimated our rhino population, a scourge that continues unabated despite concerted attempts by conservation groups and others to stem the tragic tide. Now, this threatened species has been given a lifeline: 2 000 semi-wild rhinos, once owned by a high-profile businessman and breeder, will be rewilded into reserves across the continent. It’s an audacious plan with significant risks, but the purchase of the world’s largest population of privately owned rhino could be a game-changer for these mammals. Can this ambitious conservation effort help secure a future for the white rhino?

Script:


MASA V/O: I must say I feel so fortunate to be here, I mean how many people can say they’ve been outnumbered by a threatened species like the white rhino

MASA: Over the past decade, poaching has decimated rhino numbers in Africa

Upsound: A White Rhinoceros lies dead in the Kruger National Park, South Africa
Upsound: See In the river there, there’s a rhino carcass at 12 o clock
Upsound: The way we’re carrying on, they’re going to no longer be around

In just 15 years, nearly 10,000 thousand have been slaughtered for their precious horn…in spite of a ban on the international trade of rhino horn.

Upsound: Their horn is now worth more than cocaine on the black market

Desperate times called for desperate measures. So wealthy rhino breeder John Hume came up with a controversial idea:

Pelham: [00:06:20] For more than 40 years we have sustained a notion that a ban will prevent poaching. It does not. HUME came up with the notion of let us supply horn to meet end user demand and most importantly of all, save rhinos’ lives.

It’s a dream that Hume has had for 15 years. In that time he bred over 2000 white Rhino.

But it’s a dream that’s ultimately been dashed.

Pelham: 00:12:09 effectively because of an obstructive attitude by the South African authorities. HUME was driven to bankruptcy.

Leaving the future of 15 % of the world’s population of white rhino in grave doubt…

MASA OPENING LINK: This landscape that I’m on is typically South African: flat open veld under a beating African sun but this location is special… That’s because it’s home to the world’s largest privately owned white rhino herd and their future is what this story is all about.

V/O: This 7800-hectare property situated in the North West Province, was owned by Hume who established a captive breeding operation back in 2008.

Pelham: [00:03:55] John HUME is, in our opinion, an absolute conservation hero.

V/O: Pelham Jones is the chairman of the Private Rhino Owners Association.
Masa: [00:05:40] Some people say he went into it for money. It wasn't about conserving the rhinos.
Pelham: The fact that he has bred a threatened species from where they were in terms of numbers to where they are today, he has done more for building up a rhino herd than anybody else on this earth.

V/O: But Hume’s motives were not entirely altruistic.

He made a bet that the ban on the international trade of rhino horn (that’s been in place since 1977) would be lifted, but his hopes failed to materialize and the ban remains firmly in place. As a result, he could never sell the 5 tons of horn he’d harvested over the years and became financially distressed having spent over $150 million to grow his herd.

Pelham: He was running out of time and money. He appealed internationally. He appealed to the South African government for assistance. And sadly, he got stonewalled at at every quarter.

V/O: In desperation, Hume was forced to auction the farm in April. His future and that of his 2000-strong herd of rhino would depend on finding a willing buyer.

But there were no takers

Pelham: Because of the uncertainty around rhino conservation, sadly, there were no bidders

V/O: The future of 2000 individuals of a threatened species hung in the balance


DIP TO BLACK

V/O: Then at the 11th hour, a ray of hope

Peter Fearnhead: We're familiar with John HUME and the operation.



V/O: Peter Fearnhead is CEO of African Parks, a conservation NGO with a wealth of experience managing national parks across the continent.

Peter Fearnhead: When we realised that there were no takers in the auction and it was like, okay, well what's going to happen to 2000 White Rhino? Almost certainly they would have had to have been a little bit of a fireside sale, literally. Anyone who wants a rhino come and collect a rhino. And that is not a pretty picture for the species. Finding a solution to these rhinos was a moral imperative. [00:14:52][

V/O: In September, African Parks announced the purchase of the farm for an undisclosed fee, with an audacious plan to re-wild 2000 rhino to national parks across the continent over the next 10 years.

V/O: After years of uncertainty, the future of Hume’s rhino was finally secured. In October African Parks took control of the farm and the responsibility of looking after it, falls on the shoulders of project manager Donovan Jooste

Masa: [00:07:20] What was it like taking operational control of this farm?

Donovan: [00:04:09] It was it was daunting initially. Yeah. It's a massive task. It's a massive undertaking, it's it's actually amazing to be a part of.

V/O: Our team was given exclusive TV access to the farm as we toured what was once the largest captive breeding operation in the world.

Rhino Orphanage

Donovan: So this is a breeding camp, within this camp there are about 117 rhino

Masa: Look at that! They’re so close! Oh wow





Feeding Adult rhino

V/O: In the food warehouse, the daunting nutritional requirements of 2000 rhino becomes apparent. An adult rhino requires up to 10 kg of feed daily, and food costs are astronomical.

Donovan: [00:01:45] This is where all the feeding happens. Obviously, later on in the year we go, the more we feed the lucerne over here, which comes in in about sort of four and a half thousand Rands a ton, so a bit of a hefty cost

V/O: The sheer number of rhino here is an irresistible lure for poachers. That’s why the farm’s location is kept top secret and no chances are taken with security. This includes 24-hour surveillance, rangers patrolling day and night, as well as aerial surveillance, driving up operational costs even more.

Peter Fearnhead: Maintaining this farm every single year is going to cost us approximately about 75 million Rands

V/O: And that’s before a single rhino has been relocated. While the captive breeding programme will be stopped, natural breeding will result in a total of 3000 rhino that will need to be re-located, 300 per year for the next decade

We estimate that it’s going to cost about $1,500 to move every animal within South Africa, the moment that you move into the SADC region you're talking about $5,000 per animal. And if you are moving them into Central Africa, you have to have an aerial solution. you're talking about approximately $50,000 per animal and that’s going to take a lot of time, a huge amount of effort and a huge amount of funding.
MASA: [00:08:17] Are you concerned that what ended up happening with John Hume, where he ran out of money to look after this place could happen to African Parks too?
Donovan: [00:03:05] Definitely I mean those financial challenges will always weigh heavily on us, the massive risks that we that we sit on is is making sure we do it and we do it right.
Masa: [00:26:43] When's the first translocation going to happen? [00:26:43][0.7]

Donovan: [00:27:17] We we hope to have the framework done by the by the end of this year. And we hope to do our our first relocation, our first rewilding exercise within the first two quarters of of next year.


V/O: While John Hume's controversial plan to save the rhino may have been dashed when he ran out of money, his ambition to save them lives on. He leaves behind the world's largest captive breeding project and more than 2000 of a threatened species. Could his vision yet result in the rhino's salvation?

Peter Fearnhead: [00:26:11] it is a really good news story for those 2000 rhino because there is hope for them. Obviously, now it's incumbent on African parks to complete that story and to make sure that it ends well.

Having 2000 run and their progeny in wild populations across the continent and are thriving. That is the end objective. And if we're able to achieve that, I think it's a phenomenal story, not just for rhino, but for conservation as a whole.

This is one of the largest continent-wide rewilding endeavours to occur for any species.
